brief.topic: The Geometry That Gathers a Rainbow

s01: Sunlight enters a round drop,
bends, reflects once inside,
and bends again as it leaves.
Change where the ray enters, and its exit direction changes.
But near one particular direction, something lovely happens.
Neighboring rays leave at almost the same angle.
Light gathers there.
Let us follow one ray.
At the first surface,
refraction turns it toward the inward normal.
It crosses the drop and reflects from the back.
At the final surface,
it bends away from the normal as it returns to air.
The amount of bending follows Snell's law.
For water with refractive index close to four thirds,
this path has a special turning point.
These rays enter at slightly different heights.
Notice how their outgoing directions nearly agree.
Measured from the direction straight back toward the sun,
the angle reaches a maximum near forty two degrees.
This concentration of directions

is the geometric beginning
of the primary rainbow.
It is not a claim that all the light follows one path.
Much light passes through,
and wave effects shape the fine details.
Why an arc across the sky?
Drops at the same angle

around the direction
opposite the sun
form a circle in our view.
The horizon usually hides part of it.
Different colors bend by slightly different amounts,
separating that circle into bands.
A rainbow is not a painted object waiting in one place.
It is a relationship between

sunlight, drops,
and your point of view.
